subject: psychology
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

options: A systematic tendency that distorts findings or thinking
The average of a data set
questions.explain: Bias is systematic (not random) distortion — e.g. sampling, researcher, cognitive or culture bias.

questions.q: The concept of 'perspective' reminds us that:
options: Behaviour can be viewed through different approaches and cultures, none complete
Only one culture's norms are valid
questions.explain: Perspective guards against assuming one explanation or culture is universal.

options: Ethical treatment of participants and honest interpretation
questions.explain: Responsibility includes consent, avoiding harm, and not over-claiming results.

options: Findings from one culture are wrongly assumed to be universal
A study has a large sample
questions.explain: Treating culturally specific findings as universal (imposed etic) is culture bias.

questions.q: A study samples only university students yet claims to describe 'people in general'. The main problem is:
questions.explain: An unrepresentative sample biases conclusions about the wider population.

questions.q: Reflexivity helps reduce bias by having the researcher:
options: Reflect on how their own assumptions shape the research
questions.explain: Reflexivity makes researcher influence explicit, supporting more trustworthy interpretation.

questions.q: Which design can best support a claim that one variable CAUSES another?
options: A controlled experiment with manipulation and a comparison group
questions.explain: Only experiments controlling confounds can support causal claims.

questions.q: 'Correlation does not imply causation' means a relationship between two variables:
options: Could be explained by a third variable or reverse causation
questions.explain: Association alone leaves open confounds and the direction of any causal link.

questions.q: The concept of 'change' in psychology concerns:
options: How behaviour and processes change over time
questions.explain: Change covers development, learning and plasticity, often studied longitudinally.

options: Defining it so it can be measured objectively
questions.explain: Operationalisation turns an abstract concept into a clear, measurable variable.

questions.q: Good 'measurement' requires that a measure is:
questions.explain: Measurement quality depends on consistency (reliability) and measuring the intended construct (validity).

questions.q: A correlational study reports r = 0.55 between two variables. The safest conclusion is that they:
options: Are moderately related, but causation is not established
questions.explain: A moderate positive coefficient shows association; causation needs an experiment.

questions.q: Using the key concepts in an exam answer mainly helps you to:
options: Evaluate studies critically, not just describe them
questions.explain: The concepts are analytical tools that move answers from description to evaluation.

questions.q: To study whether an intervention CHANGES behaviour over two years, the strongest design is:
options: A longitudinal study (ideally with a comparison group)
questions.explain: Tracking the same people over time captures change; a comparison group strengthens causal inference.

questions.q: Which concept is most directly about honest, ethical use of psychology?
questions.explain: Responsibility covers ethics and honest interpretation and application of findings.

questions.q: A very large sample can make even a tiny effect statistically significant, which shows the importance of also considering:
questions.explain: Significance is not importance; effect size and practical relevance matter too.

questions.q: A headline says a study 'proves' a food cures anxiety, based on a small correlational survey. The best critique uses:
questions.explain: Naming causality and bias exposes the over-claim from weak correlational evidence.

options: Offers an alternative explanation for the results
Is the same as the dependent variable
questions.explain: Confounds threaten causal claims by providing rival explanations.

specSource: IB Diploma Psychology guide (first assessment 2027); Core concepts (bias, causality, change, measurement, perspective, responsibility)
